newsitem.title: CANADA: More cool places to hang on Web?.
newsitem.headline: More cool places to hang on Web?.

text.p: The house that is the World Wide Web is in need of a bit more space.
Right now it seems everyone wants to hang out in the same room -- that is the "Dot Com" entity.
Many a corporation, and a few other groups besides, want their Web addresses to end in ".com" and a number of dust-ups have already occurred in the courts over who can use what name.

There are three generic domain name groupings (otherwise known as generic top level domain names) in use: ".org," ".net" and ".com." But of course everyone is trying to squeeze into the commercial grouping. In fact, several thousand addresses are added daily to the .com category, according to the Internet Society.
So a bunch of really august organizations, led by the Internet Society, last week announced plans to add seven new domain names, which could take effect later this year.

Something called the International Ad Hoc Committee was formed last year to deal with this issue. It will hold a meeting in Geneva at the end of April to gain broadspread support for the new domain names.
The proposed categories are:
- .firm (for businesses or firms)
- .store (for those wishing to sell things)
- .web (for those wanting to emphasize Web activities)
- .arts (for those involved in the arts)
- .rec (for those involved in sports and recreation)
- .info (for those dealing in information)
- .nom (for individual or personal nomenclature)
Interested parties can surf over to the Ad Hoc's site (www.iahc.org) to get more information, but be warned, the reading can be heavy going at times.

The Ad Hoc's final report contained this illuminating sentence: "gTLD administration and management will comprise multiple competing registrars, globally dispersed, under a Council of Registrars (CORE) established by a Memorandum of Understanding (CORE-MoU) which is signed by the registrars. CORE will operate as a Swiss nonprofit association."
The Ad Hoc group comes across as a ponderous organization. But, to be fair, it is also dealing with other weighty and bureaucratic groups to get this all through.
These new names are incredibly important when you consider these committees are essentially creating new lands for pioneers to inhabit in this budding digital world.

We will have to see if the category ".firm" will have the same cachet as the ".com" group and provide more space for commercial entities to set up. Would a Microsoft Corp. be just as happy to have an address ending in "dot firm" instead of the vaunted "dot com" for instance?
Officials at the Internet Society said they were inundated with hundreds of ideas on what new domain names should be created to accommodate the growth of the Web.
Some people had suggested the Web needed a ".sex" category to house the burgeoning adult trade on the Internet. But the Ad Hoc group appeared to have rejected the category for one reason or another.

It could be argued that adding ".sex" would have only encouraged the sex trade on the Net, while others might say such a category would help prevent people from stumbling unwittingly into those areas.

The other newly minted sectors, however, should give some breathing room for other non-corporate groups looking to expand on the Net. Arts and sporting groups might really appreciate the ".art" and ".rec" groups to show they are different from companies wanting to sell art or sporting goods.
Perhaps ".nom" for nomenclature could be the most interesting. It has an eclectic feel to it that individual surfers might like to use in their personal addresses for their home sites on the Web.
So perhaps soon it will be passe to ask for e-mail addresses. Instead, it will be: "Like, what's your Dot Nom?"
